## The incident

In 1981 T.J. Hamblin wrote a Christmas article for the BMJ titled "Fake!" He described spinach as a case study: "The discovery that spinach was as valuable a source of iron as red meat was made in the 1890s. Unfortunately, the propaganda was fraudulent; German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value."

Hamblin's article listed 13 references. None of them documented the decimal point error.

The story did not originate with Hamblin. In 1972, A.E. Bender, speaking at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London, had said: "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Bender hedged the claim.

## Who lied

Nobody. Bender hedged. Hamblin stated it as fact, unsourced. Sutton reports that when he asked Hamblin for the source, Hamblin replied he had been asked to write a humorous Christmas article without references and could not recall the origin. Hamblin assured Sutton he had not invented it.

In 1995 Lennart Larsson published "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation," warning against repeating claims without scrutinizing their sources. Larsson's paper repeated the spinach story, citing Hamblin, providing none of his own.

Sutton searched for weeks: electronic databases, biochemistry specialists, archives. He could not name the German chemists, could not locate the original measurement, could not establish when the error supposedly occurred. Different versions of the story placed it at 1870, the 1890s, or the 1930s. Øyvind Rekdal, analyzing the citation chain, found that sources "have mutually confirmed the 'fact' that a decimal point error was made, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s."

## The bit continues

Rekdal's 2014 analysis of academic legend found the irony stark: "By using the non-existent, or at least undocumented, decimal point error as an illustration of the importance of accuracy and critical investigation, Bender, Hamblin, Larsson, and Skrabanek and McCormick all end up doing the opposite of what they are preaching."

The story remains in circulation. It serves as the textbook example of an uncorrected error and of how scientific claims propagate without scrutiny. Both descriptions are true. The example itself has no documented source.

## The incident

For decades the spinach story has been the textbook case of an error nobody corrected. In the 1890s, it goes, a decimal point went in the wrong place and made spinach look 10 times richer in iron than it is.

The most quoted telling is Hamblin's "Fake!", a BMJ Christmas piece from 19 December 1981. It says German chemists "had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value." That paragraph has no citation. The article ends with 13 publications it "derived from", none about spinach. Sutton reports that none of them "cite the source of the decimal error or 1930's Germans".

The earliest version Rekdal found is older. Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London, said the fame of spinach "may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point". Tellings disagree on when the error happened. Rekdal notes "a large number of apparently independent sources" that "mutually confirmed" it, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s.

## Who lied

The papers do not accuse anyone. Bender hedged. Kronick's 1985 version also hedges: "It has been suggested that..." Hamblin stated the story as fact.

Sutton emailed Hamblin. Sutton reports that Hamblin "wrote that he has been asked for this before and that he honestly cannot remember," and that in 1981 the BMJ's editor had asked him for a humorous Christmas piece and "asked not to provide references." Hamblin closed by assuring Sutton that he was "sure that he had not made it up."

Sutton's search for the source found nothing. He asked "Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded?" and, after weeks of searching, could not answer. He also read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. Of hundreds of Popeye cartoons, he reports, none links spinach to iron. The strip of 3 July 1932, where Popeye first explains why he eats spinach, credits vitamin A. "In fact, Segar chose and promoted spinach for its vitamin A content alone," Sutton concludes.

Larsson's 1995 paper, "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation", repeats the story and cites Hamblin.

## The bit continues

Rekdal's open-access paper opens by citing Larsson, then admits: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." His conclusion on the whole chain: "By using the non-existent, or at least undocumented, decimal point error as an illustration of the importance of accuracy and critical investigation, Bender, Hamblin, Larsson, and Skrabanek and McCormick all end up doing the opposite of what they are preaching."

In the BMJ's Christmas issue of 19 December 1981, under the heading "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes", T.J. Hamblin wrote that the discovery that spinach was as valuable a source of iron as red meat was made in the 1890s.

"Unfortunately, the propaganda was fraudulent; German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value. Spinach is no better for you than cabbage, Brussels sprouts, or broccoli. For a source of iron Popeye would have been better off chewing the cans."

The paragraph carries no citation. The article closes with a list of 13 publications it was derived from. None is about spinach.

## Who lied

Nobody, and the hedging is in the record. The earliest version Rekdal traced is Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London: the fame of spinach "may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point". Kronick, in 1985, wrote "It has been suggested that spinach got its reputation as a dietary supplement because of a misplaced decimal point". Hamblin stated it without a source.

Sutton, a criminologist at Nottingham Trent University, emailed him. Sutton reports that Hamblin wrote he had been asked for this before and honestly could not remember, that the then editor of the BMJ had asked him for a humorous piece for the Christmas edition, and that he had been asked not to provide references. Sutton adds that Hamblin "rounded off his email with the assurance that he was sure that he had not made it up."

In 1995, in the Journal of Internal Medicine, Larsson repeated the story and cited Hamblin. The paper was titled "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation".

## The bit continues

Sutton spent weeks on 4 questions. Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded. Who were the 1930s chemists. He answered none of them. The nearest thing to an origin he found was a 2009 Royal Society of Chemistry textbook offering 2 incompatible versions: von Bunge in 1890 measuring 35mg per 100g of spinach that had been dried, or von Wolf misplacing a decimal point about 20 years earlier.

Dried spinach has been measured at 44.8 mg of iron per 100 g in 1938 and about 34 mg in 2009. The USDA lists raw spinach at 2.71 mg per 100 g. A dried sample read as a fresh one produces a tenfold error without anyone moving a decimal point.

Sutton also read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. In the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains why he eats spinach, he credits vitamin A. Of the hundreds of Popeye cartoons Sutton studied, none associates spinach with iron.

## The incident

The story: A decimal point error made spinach's reputation for iron. Someone measuring spinach in the 1890s (or 1870s, or 1930s, depending on who tells it) placed a decimal incorrectly, making the iron content 10 times higher than it actually was. German chemists corrected it, and the error became a textbook example of how sloppy science travels unchecked.

Hamblin wrote in the BMJ in 1981: "The discovery that spinach was as valuable a source of iron as red meat was made in the 1890s. Unfortunately, the propaganda was fraudulent; German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value."

## Who lied

Nobody. Bender introduced it in 1972, hedged: the fame of spinach "may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Hamblin restated it in 1981 as settled fact, but offered no source. The article containing the claim had 13 references; none addressed the decimal error.

"Hamblin wrote that he has been asked for this before and that he honestly cannot remember," Sutton reports. "He said that back in 1981 he had been asked to write a humorous piece by the then editor of the British Medical Journal for its Christmas edition and that he had been asked not to provide references."

Sutton, a criminology reader at Nottingham Trent, spent weeks in 2010 searching for the original. He could not answer basic questions: "Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded?" He found no chemist names, no primary documents, no proof the error ever happened as described.

Larsson repeated the story in 1995 in an article titled "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation." Rekdal notes: "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way." Rekdal himself opens his own paper by citing Larsson's Hamblin reference, then pauses: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." He does this deliberately, to show how readily a doubtful claim travels.

## The bit continues

The story endures. It is cited as a cautionary tale: evidence of how citation errors compound when no one checks the original source. Yet the original source has never been produced. Bender hedged in 1972. Hamblin stated it without evidence in 1981. Larsson repeated it in 1995 while warning others against repeating unverified claims. Each time the story moved further from its supposed origin.

Rekdal's examination captures the irony: "By using the non-existent, or at least undocumented, decimal point error as an illustration of the importance of accuracy and critical investigation, Bender, Hamblin, Larsson, and Skrabanek and McCormick all end up doing the opposite of what they are preaching."

"The discovery that spinach was as valuable a source of iron as red meat was made in the 1890s ... The paragraph carries no citation. The article closes with the 13 publications it was derived from. None of them is about spinach.

The earliest telling Rekdal found hedges. Arnold Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London: "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point". Hamblin stated it, and gave no source.

In 1995 the Journal of Internal Medicine published Larsson's "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation". It repeats the spinach story and cites Hamblin. Rekdal: "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way."

Mike Sutton, a criminologist at Nottingham Trent University, emailed Hamblin in 2010. Sutton reports that Hamblin "wrote that he has been asked for this before and that he honestly cannot remember", that the BMJ's editor had commissioned a humorous piece for the Christmas edition and asked him "not to provide references", and that he "rounded off his email with the assurance that he was sure that he had not made it up."

## The bit continues

Sutton set himself 4 questions, among them "Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded?" and who the 1930s chemists were. Weeks of searching answered none of them. The tellings do not agree on when the error happened: Rekdal records 1870, the 1890s, and the 1930s.

There is a real measurement underneath. Sutton quotes Coultate's 2009 Royal Society of Chemistry book, which offers 2 versions: von Bunge in 1890 found 35mg per 100g but had analysed dried spinach, or von Wolf misplaced a decimal point about 20 years earlier. Dried spinach does run that high. Sutton cites 44.8 mg per 100 g from Jackson in 1938 and about 34 mg from Oladele and Obarisaide in 2009. USDA puts raw spinach at 2.71 mg. Drying to raw is already a factor of roughly 10, with the decimal point in place.

Popeye was never the evidence. Sutton read the bound Thimble Theatre volumes from 1928 to 1935 and reports that in the first strip where Popeye explains why he eats spinach, 3 July 1932, he credits vitamin A.

## The incident

For decades, nutrition writers have repeated a specific story: spinach was once hailed as rich in iron because a researcher misplaced a decimal point and reported 10 times the true amount. The earliest version found is hedged. In a 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, Bender wrote that the vegetable's fame "may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point."

Hamblin's 1981 BMJ Christmas piece, "Fake!", dropped the hedge. German chemists, he wrote, had reinvestigated in the 1930s and found "the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate." Spinach, he concluded, was no better for you than cabbage, Brussels sprouts, or broccoli; Popeye would have done better chewing the can.

Later tellers cannot agree even on the year. Rekdal counts versions dated 1870, the 1890s, and the 1930s, independently confirming a fact none of them had traced to a document.

## Who lied

Nobody, on the documented record. Bender hedged. Hamblin stated the claim as fact and attached no citation; his article closes with a list of 13 references, and Sutton, checking in 2010, found that none of them "cite the source of the decimal error or 1930's Germans." Bender's 1972 lecture predates Hamblin's, so the story did not start with him.

Sutton emailed Hamblin directly. Sutton reports that Hamblin wrote back that he had been asked to write something humorous for the BMJ's Christmas issue and told not to supply references, that he could no longer remember his source, and that he was "sure that he had not made it up."

Larsson repeated the story in 1995, in a paper titled "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation," citing Hamblin. Sutton went looking for the underlying measurement anyway: who was von Wolff, where were his findings, who were the 1930s chemists. Weeks of searching answered none of it. He found two candidate origins instead, via Coultate's 2009 account: either von Bunge measured 35mg per 100g in 1890 but had analysed dried spinach, or von Wolf misplaced a decimal some 20 years earlier. Dried spinach measured later came in at 44.8mg per 100g (Jackson, 1938) and about 34mg per 100g (Oladele and Obarisaide, 2009); raw spinach today is listed at 2.71mg per 100g (USDA). The tenfold gap the story blames on a typo is roughly the gap between dried and fresh.

Sutton also read the Popeye newspaper strips, 1928 to 1935. None of them tie spinach to iron. Creator Segar's own strip, 3 July 1932, credits the vegetable's vitamin A instead.

## The bit continues

Rekdal opens his own 2014 paper by citing Larsson for the Hamblin reference, then tells readers: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." His verdict covers the whole chain: Bender, Hamblin, Larsson, and Skrabanek and McCormick, all writing about the importance of accurate citation, "end up doing the opposite of what they are preaching." No correction to the BMJ piece has surfaced. The story is still told as the standard case of an error nobody caught.

## The incident

The story: a decimal point slipped, and spinach was credited with 10 times the iron it has. It is told as the standard example of a scientific error nobody corrected.

The earliest version Rekdal found is Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London: "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point". Kronick, in 1985, also hedged: "It has been suggested that spinach got its reputation as a dietary supplement because of a misplaced decimal point."

The BMJ Christmas issue of 1981 dropped the hedge. T.J. Hamblin wrote that German chemists "had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate". Spinach, he added, was "no better for you than cabbage, Brussels sprouts, or broccoli."

The paragraph has no citation. The article lists 13 references. Sutton counted the same 13 and found that none of them cites the source of the decimal error or the 1930s Germans.

## Who lied

No institution has said anyone did. The article's own framing was "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes".

Mike Sutton, a criminologist at Nottingham Trent University, asked who von Wolff was, where his erroneous findings were recorded, and who the 1930s chemists were. After weeks of searching he could not answer. He emailed Hamblin. Sutton reports that Hamblin replied that he had been asked before and could not remember, that the BMJ editor had asked for a humorous piece without references, and that he was sure he had not made it up.

Bender's 1972 lecture precedes Hamblin, so the trail does not start in 1981. The dates do not agree either. Rekdal: "a large number of apparently independent sources have mutually confirmed the 'fact' that a decimal point error was made, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s."

Sutton cites Coultate's 2009 book for 2 competing versions. In one, von Bunge found 35 mg of iron per 100 g in 1890 but had analysed dried spinach. Sutton cites dried-spinach measurements of 44.8 mg per 100 g (Jackson, 1938). USDA lists raw spinach at 2.71 mg.

## The bit continues

In 1995 Larsson published "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation" in the Journal of Internal Medicine. It repeats the spinach story and cites Hamblin. Rekdal: "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way."

Rekdal opens his own paper by citing Larsson, then states: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." He meant it as a demonstration.

Sutton also read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. He reports that the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains why he eats spinach, credits vitamin A, and that in hundreds of strips none links spinach to iron.

Someone put the decimal point in the wrong place, making spinach appear 10 times richer in iron than it is. The error went uncorrected for decades and spawned Popeye.

T.J. Hamblin told this version in the BMJ's 1981 Christmas issue: "German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value."

## The incident

In December 1981 the BMJ's Christmas issue ran "Fake!" by T.J. Hamblin, a survey of "Frauds, hoaxes, fakes, and widely popularised mistakes". A single paragraph covered spinach. Its reputation as a source of iron, Hamblin wrote, dated from the 1890s, and "the propaganda was fraudulent; German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value." His conclusion: "For a source of iron Popeye would have been better off chewing the cans."

The paragraph has no citation. The article lists 13 publications it was "derived from". None is about spinach.

## Who lied

Nobody, on the record. Hamblin was not the first. The earliest version Rekdal (2014) found is from Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London: "the fame of spinach may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Kronick in 1985 was also hedged: "It has been suggested." Hamblin dropped the hedge and gave no source.

Sutton, a Reader in Criminology at Nottingham Trent University, emailed Hamblin. Sutton reports that Hamblin "honestly cannot remember", that the BMJ's editor had asked him for a humorous Christmas piece and asked him "not to provide references", and that Hamblin was "sure that he had not made it up."

The tellings disagree on the date. Rekdal: sources "mutually confirmed the 'fact' that a decimal point error was made, whether it was in 1870, in the 1890s, or in the 1930s." Sutton quotes a 2009 Royal Society of Chemistry book offering 2 versions: a decimal point misplaced about 20 years before 1890, or von Bunge reporting 35 mg per 100 g in 1890 from dried spinach. Sutton cites dried-spinach measurements of 44.8 mg per 100 g (1938) and about 34 (2009). The USDA lists raw spinach at 2.71. On the second version, the high figure was a correct measurement of dried spinach.

In 1995 Larsson published "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation" in the Journal of Internal Medicine. It repeats the spinach story, citing Hamblin. Rekdal: "Larsson obviously has an important message, but he manages to do exactly what he is criticizing others for in quite a spectacular way."

## The fix

Sutton went looking. Among his questions: "Who is von Wolff and where are his erroneous findings recorded?" and who the 1930s chemists were. Weeks of searching produced no answers.

He also read the Thimble Theatre strips from 1928 to 1935. In the strip of 3 July 1932, the first in which Popeye explains why he eats spinach, the reason is vitamin A. Of "hundreds of Popeye cartoons studied", Sutton reports, none links spinach to iron.

Rekdal opened his 2014 paper on academic urban legends by citing Larsson, then disclosed his method: "In short, I have plagiarized the Hamblin reference from Larsson." It was a demonstration.

Decades later, German scientists corrected the error, but by then spinach had its reputation. In some versions Popeye was involved.

The story is usually told to illustrate the danger of uncorrected scientific mistakes. It is also uncorrected, and it has no source.

T.J. Hamblin wrote it in the BMJ in 1981. His article, titled "Fake!" and published in the Christmas issue, listed 13 references. None supported the spinach claim. The passage: "The discovery that spinach was as valuable a source of iron as red meat was made in the 1890s... Unfortunately, the propaganda was fraudulent; German chemists reinvestigating the iron content of spinach had shown in the 1930s that the original workers had put the decimal point in the wrong place and made a tenfold overestimate of its value."

Mike Sutton, a criminologist at Nottingham Trent, searched for the original measurement. He read papers, databases, and the original Popeye strips from 1928 to 1935. He emailed Hamblin in 2010. Sutton reports that Hamblin said he could not remember where he got the story and was sure he had not made it up. Hamblin also said the BMJ editor had asked him not to provide references.

Nobody, on the record. The record contains people stating the story, hedging about it, and failing to find its source.

The earliest version Ole Bjørn Rekdal traced was Arnold Bender's 1972 inaugural lecture at Queen Elizabeth College, University of London. Bender hedged: the fame of spinach "may well have grown from a misplaced decimal point." Hamblin stated it as fact in 1981, with no citation. In 1995 Sture Larsson repeated it in the Journal of Internal Medicine, citing Hamblin. The paper's title: "The dissemination of false data through inadequate citation."

Rekdal, writing in 2014 about academic urban legends, admitted he copied the Hamblin reference from Larsson without checking it, as a deliberate demonstration. His line: "By using the non-existent, or at least undocumented, decimal point error as an illustration of the importance of accuracy and critical investigation, Bender, Hamblin, Larsson, and Skrabanek and McCormick all end up doing the opposite of what they are preaching."

The year of the supposed error varies by telling. Rekdal catalogued versions placing it in 1870, the 1890s, or the 1930s.

Sutton found a competing explanation. The high figure may be a real measurement of dried spinach, which concentrates iron, later read as fresh. The USDA lists raw spinach at 2.71 milligrams of iron per 100 grams.

Sutton also checked Popeye. The first strip where Popeye explains why he eats spinach, 3 July 1932, credits vitamin A. Of hundreds of cartoons Sutton studied, none mentioned iron.

The story is still told. Rekdal's paper, citing it as an example of uncorrected error, was published in 2014. The original 19th-century measurement it describes has never been produced.
